<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>The end of __get_user() and __put_user()</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>Linus Torvalds rarely writes significant amounts of kernel code these days, so
the <a
href="https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=22a78a25438d">merging</a>
of a 48-part patch series from him is an unusual event.  This series,
destined for the 7.4 kernel release, performs some long-delayed kernel
cleanup by removing a couple of the primitives used to access user-space memory
from the kernel.  What was once a best practice has long been superseded,
but it can take time for such changes to work their way through a body of
code this large.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Rust features in the future</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
There are several Rust features that kernel developers have been hoping to
stabilize, but Josh Triplett wanted to describe all of the <em>other</em>
features that the Rust project is currently working on. He spoke about the topic
at Kangrejos 2026, leaving the assembled kernel developers with several ideas
about how to use these upcoming Rust features in the kernel.
The features included refinements to the type system, small syntax improvements, and a
smarter borrow checker.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Seeking smaller kernel stacks</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</guid>
			<dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
			<description>Memory has always been a scarce resource in computing systems, but the
problem seems to have worsened recently.  In particular, the worldwide
shortage of memory chips has led to a renewed focus by systems developers
on reducing memory usage.  During the memory-management microconference at
the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>, Will
Deacon discussed one specific consumer of memory that is being
re-examined: kernel stacks.
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">

			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/</guid>

			<description><p>
Since the merge window for 7.4 opened, there have been 6,753 non-merge
changesets pulled into the mainline repository. Many more are expected,

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Python's experimental JIT to be removed</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p>Python's <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3.13/whatsnew/3.13.html#an-experimental-just-in-time-jit-compiler">experimental
just-in-time (JIT) compiler</a>, which was added to CPython in 2024 for the <a
href="https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3130/">3.13&#160;release</a>,
is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council <a
href="https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638">announced</a>
that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an
accepted <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0001">Python Enhancement
Proposal</a> (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and
set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating
<a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0836/">PEP&#160;836</a> ("JIT Go Brrr: The
Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython")
to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the
JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on
the once-promising project has come to an end.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>Guidelines for panics in kernel code</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100873/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100873/</guid>
			<dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
			<description><p>
Alexandre Courbot spends most of his time working on the kernel doing code
reviews. Recently, he's been wondering about what the standards should be for
when Rust code is allowed to panic, and how it should do error handling more
generally. Unlike many of the other talks at Kangrejos 2026, his talk was not
presenting some existing work, but rather hoping to solicit opinions on the
topic from the assembled Rust for Linux developers. He brought along a collection of tricky
cases that he had run into recently to prompt discussion.
</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
			<title>The campaign to push Northstar into Linux distributions</title>
			<link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102738/</link>
			<guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102738/</guid>
			<dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
			<description><p>There is not a broad selection of mature, open-source web-browser engines
for Linux users. Most of the browsers available for Linux are based on one of
just three projects: Chromium's <a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink_(browser_engine)">Blink</a>, Firefox's
<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gecko_(software)">Gecko</a>, or <a
href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebKit">WebKit</a>. A new entrant would
generally be seen as a welcome alternative, but the recent campaign to push one
of the LLM-written <a href="https://nordstjernen.org/">Nordstjernen</a> browsers
into <a href="https://debian.org/">Debian</a> and  <a
href="https://archlinux.org/">Arch Linux</a> has raised some questions about
the project's development and security processes.</p>
</description>
			<pubDate>Thu, 05 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
		</item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Containers as a recognized kernel object</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102593/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102593/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The foundation of the design for containers in the kernel is that there
isn't one; there is no container abstraction that the kernel recognizes.
Instead, the kernel provides a long list of components — namespaces,
control groups, sandboxing mechanisms, and more — along with a note that
says, in effect, "some assembly required".  There have been <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/723477/">attempts</a> (<a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/780364/">repeatedly</a>) over the years to turn containers
into first-class objects with kernel support, but they have never gotten
far.  Now Josef Bacik is <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261026-cells-rfc-v2-b41d7e0c95a3@toxicpanda.com">making a
try</a> with a concept that he calls "cells".
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>System-call wrappers for glibc</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101647/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101647/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>In a followup to his 
<a href="https://lpc.events/event/19/contributions/2220/">session at the
2025 Linux Plumbers Conference</a> (LPC), Carlos O'Donell returned to the topic
of <a href="https://lpc.events/event/20/contributions/2397/">system-call
wrappers for the GNU C library</a> (glibc) at this year's event.  This time
around, he was joined by Florian Weimer, who is another glibc maintainer.
The idea was to give an update on what has happened over the last year with
regard to Linux system calls that lack a glibc wrapper, thus are only
accessible via
<a
href="https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html"><tt>syscall()</tt></a>.  In addition, they wanted to hear from attendees about their
needs in this area.
</description>

        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Removing binder.c</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102982/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102982/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation
of Android's
<a href="https://source.android.com/docs/core/architecture/ipc/binder-overview">
Binder driver</a>, the primary interprocess communication mechanism
used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C
code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into
replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust
implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most
difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>The second part of the 7.4 merge window</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102739/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102739/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The 7.4 merge window, which
<a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1104653/">closed</a> on November 1,
included a record-breaking 18,591 non-merge changesets.
That is almost as many as the entire 7.3 development cycle, which had 18,765, itself a record breaker. Of
those, 11,838 landed after <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/">the article covering the
first part of the merge window</a>. Most of those were bug fixes of
various forms; it seems as though bug fixes may be crowding out feature
additions <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1104210/">across the open-source ecosystem</a> to
some extent. Still, a good number of new features were included, and a handful
removed, in the tail end of the merge window.
</p>
</description>

        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>LLM reviews for Debian's new queue spark debate</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103674/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103674/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>The Debian project has wrestled with the topic of LLM usage for years, which
culminated in a <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1087134/">general-resolution
vote</a> this August. The project <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1091231/">voted in favor</a> of the fifth, out of
eight, option: "<a
href="https://www.debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002#texte">Responsible Use of
Generative AI</a>". With the door open to LLM use, the <a
href="https://wiki.debian.org/Teams/DFSG">DFSG, Licensing &amp; New Packages
Team</a> (usually shortened to "DFSG team"), which is <a
href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1043364/">relatively new</a>, has started to employ LLMs in
sending out reviews of packages entering Debian's <a href="https://wiki.debian.org/NewQueue?pow_referer=https%3A%2F%2Fkagi.com%2F">new queue</a>. The practice has
raised a number of objections and questions about where lines should be drawn in
the use of LLM-generated output.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Portable Python scripts with dependencies</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1104646/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1104646/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>A basic Python script is portable: it can be copied between machines with little concern about compatibility.
A script that depends on third-party packages requires quite a bit more
care and consideration, however.
In 2023, <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0723/">PEP
723</a> ("Inline script metadata") introduced a standard for declaring a Python script's
dependencies inside the script itself.
Several third-party tools can now automatically install and manage those dependencies, but there is still little official support for this standard within Python itself.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Plasma X11 session removal surprises some Fedora users</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105130/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1105130/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>The KDE Project announced, in&#160;2025, that <a
href="https://kde.org/announcements/plasma/6/6.7.0/">Plasma&#160;6.7</a> would
be the last version of the desktop environment that would support X11
sessions. Those who keep up with KDE's announcements no doubt expected it when
<a href="https://kde.org/announcements/plasma/6/6.8.0/">Plasma&#160;6.8</a>
dropped X11 support as promised. What seems to have come as a surprise, at
least to a number of <a href="https://fedoraproject.org/kde/">Fedora KDE Plasma
Desktop</a> users, is that the Fedora&#160;44 release&mdash;which shipped in
April with <a
href="https://kde.org/announcements/plasma/6/6.6.0/">Plasma&#160;6.6</a>&mdash;received
an update to Plasma&#160;6.8 that swept away the X11 session without much warning.
Despite the surprise, it is gone for good: the <a
href="https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/fesco/">Fedora Engineering Steering
Committee</a> (FESCo) has <a
href="https://forge.fedoraproject.org/fesco/tickets/issues/3707#issuecomment-1371370">voted
against</a> a request to revert the update for Fedora 44 and the just-released
Fedora 45.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 12 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>User namespaces + file capabilities = trouble</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103429/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103429/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description><a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/532593/">User namespaces</a> are a key part of the
kernel's toolkit for assembling containers; processes within a user
namespace can appear to have full root access to the system while gaining
no extra privileges in the wider system.  At least, that is the intent.  In
practice, keeping privilege contained within a user namespace has often
turned out to be difficult.  As an example, consider <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20261027-b4-setfcap-userns-v8-0-2674adc63f3c@toxicpanda.com">this
small patch series</a> from Josef Bacik, which is intended to address some
situations where a process within a user namespace can elevate the
privileges of processes outside of it.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

<item xmlns:dc="http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/">
        <title>Locking down hibernation for the winter</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103190/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1103190/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and
then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data
back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off.
Unfortunately, the kernel does not have
any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with,
which is why <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/791863/">lockdown</a>, an optional kernel
feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation.
Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/linux-pm/20261008132532.1155166-1-matthewg@nvidia.com/">
a patch set</a> that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect
against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older
kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
